newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-STYLE MATTERS FOR PROUD ITALIANS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-STYLE MATTERS FOR PROUD ITALIANS.

text.p: Cesare Maldini was mistaken, although no one in Italy is saying so.

After the four-nation Tournoi de France, in which his country finished last and let in more goals than any of their opponents, Italy's coach and his men headed for home on Thursday amid applause and admiration.
"Azzurri with their heads held high," declared the daily Gazzetta dello Sport in a front page headline.
"Italian Pride," said Tuttosport. "Proudly Italian," added the Corriere dello Sport.
Surely there was some mistake. Italy had failed to win a match, conceded seven goals and lost 2-0 to England whom they play in a World Cup qualifier later this year.
As Maldini warned beforehand, speaking to compatriots once famous for flinging tomatoes at returning players and coaches who failed to live up to national expectations, Italians do not like losing.
"Everyone says the results don't matter at the beginning but then if we lose it will be like the end of the world," Maldini said as the team left for France.
The subsequent evidence showed he was wrong and that, as so often in Italy where soccer brings everything to a grinding halt, style is every bit as important.
Yes, Italy lost and did not win a match. But they played world champions Brazil with such style and determination that it did not matter. Italians were proud.
They also scored as many goals as Brazil and striker Alessandro del Piero was top scorer with three goals -- England's final total.
The break with the past was noticeable.

Maldini's predecessor Arrigo Sacchi reached the World Cup final in 1994, losing on penalties to Brazil, but that achievement lifted few hearts in an Italy yearning for the stirring days of Paolo Rossi.
Under Sacchi, the team could win and still get booed, accused of boringly workmanlike performances that lacked "fantasia," the creative flair that Italians long for.
Maldini, on old-fashioned coach who was sidekick to Italy's 1982 World Cup winning coach Enzo Bearzot, has brought back the feelgood factor.

Struggling and stressed under Sacchi, Italy seem to have cast off their constraints. They head their World Cup qualifying group and before the Tournoi had not conceded a goal or lost a match under Maldini.
"I must compliment everybody and Cesare who is really doing a great job," said former coach Azeglio Vicini.
"Thank you, and in no small measure, to Cesare Maldini's Italy which won the admiration and love of fans worldwide for the match against Brazil," declared Tuttosport.
Soccer federation head Luciano Nizzola called the tournament useful and added: "They were all good, starting with Cesare Maldini who knew how to motivate a tired group."
The 3-3 draw against Brazil was a cathartic match for Italian soccer that atoned for years of frustration.
It was the first time in 14 years Italy had conceded three goals but it was also deemed the best game by the national team for at least as long.
Both Gigi Riva, the top international goalscorer in Italian soccer history, and World Cup-winning midfielder Marco Tardelli listed it as one of the five best ever played.
"All in all, we came out well," said Maldini after Italy closed with a fighting 2-2 draw with France.
"We lost only the first match but I don't want to talk about that, which happened because we were not fully prepared."
